events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Leo proposes Leo, Zara. I’ll join Zara for the first mission; this team gives us a straightforward starting point.

I’m not ready to approve Leo and Zara just because it is the first mission. Leo’s explanation is thin: “a straightforward starting point” does not explain why Zara specifically, and with one Fail enough to sink Mission 1, the bar for the first team should be higher. Zara, did you have any prior reason to expect Leo would choose you, or did Leo give you any signal before this proposal?

Priya, to answer directly: I had no prior reason to expect Leo would pick me, and Leo gave me no private signal before the proposal. I learned I was on the team when it was announced publicly. I can't speak to Leo's reasoning beyond what Leo has said here. Since I'm on this team, you should weigh my view with that in mind. I'd like Leo to explain more specifically why this pairing fits the first mission, since the thin rationale you flagged is a fair concern.

Zara has answered my earlier question directly, but the core issue remains unresolved: Leo’s explanation for this exact pairing is still thin. Leo, please give a concrete reason why Zara specifically was chosen over Felix or Isha, and explain what makes Leo and Zara safer than the alternatives when a single Fail card sinks Mission 1. If the answer is only that it is a straightforward starting point, I will not be persuaded to approve this team.

Priya, there was no prior signal or specific evidence behind choosing Zara over Felix or Isha. I included myself because I know I will play Success, and chose Zara as a starting point, not because I can demonstrate that Zara is safer than the alternatives. I understand why that isn’t enough to reassure everyone, but I’m willing to stand by the team and learn from the vote and mission result.

Leo has now confirmed there was no specific reason for choosing Zara over Felix or Isha, and no prior signal between them. That leaves the proposed team resting only on Leo’s self-assertion that Leo will play Success. Zara answered my earlier question directly, and I do not blame Zara for Leo’s thin rationale, but with a single Fail able to sink Mission 1, I cannot treat “a starting point” as sufficient. I will vote against this team unless Leo revises it and gives a more concrete basis for the exact pairing.

I agree with Priya that the rationale behind this pairing is weak. Leo has essentially admitted there was no concrete reasoning for choosing Zara over Felix or me — just that it was a "starting point." That concerns me. If both of you are good, the mission succeeds regardless, but we don't have that assurance. I'd prefer Leo revise this team to include players we have stronger reasons to trust, rather than a team built on no particular logic. Felix, you haven't weighed in yet — do you have any concerns about this pairing, or do you think Leo and Zara is a safe bet for Mission 1?

Isha asked me directly, so here is my answer: yes, I have concerns about this pairing. Mission 1 fails on a single Fail card, so the bar for a two-person team should be high, and right now the only thing holding Leo and Zara together is Leo's self-declared certainty that Leo will play Success. That is not evidence I can weigh — every player at this table could say the same words. What actually matters is what we learned in this discussion: Leo has openly confirmed there was no specific reason to choose Zara over anyone else, no prior signal, and no basis for claiming Zara is safer than Felix, Isha, or Priya. I appreciate the honesty, but honesty about having no rationale is still no rationale. To be clear, I do not think this makes Zara suspicious — Zara answered Priya's questions directly and candidly, and Zara was chosen, not choosing. The weakness here sits with the proposal itself, not with Zara's conduct. My concern is simply that a team assembled arbitrarily gives us no information either way, and on a mission this fragile, arbitrary is a risk we do not need to take when we still have the chance to build a team with some actual reasoning behind it. I would rather see Leo revise the team to a pairing that comes with a concrete justification — shared reasoning about who has given us reason for confidence, or a deliberate structure we can evaluate — than vote approval on a coin flip. Leo, you said you are willing to stand by this team and learn from the vote, but you still hold the chance to revise once before we all vote. Will you revise this team to a pairing with an actual stated basis, or are you asking us to approve a team whose only justification is that someone had to be picked first? If your answer is that you are keeping it as is, then I will vote accordingly, and the table will have its answer about this proposal one way or the other.

Felix, I’m keeping Leo and Zara. There is no proven safe pairing at this stage, and changing the team would not create evidence of safety by itself. Zara answered directly and acknowledged the limits of what she could know about my choice. That is a modest reason to keep her, not proof of her alignment. I’ll stand by the proposal and let the vote give us information to evaluate.

Leo has now given his final answer, and it changes nothing essential. His defense of keeping this team comes down to two claims: that there is no proven safe pairing at this stage, and that revising the team would not create evidence of safety by itself. I want to address both honestly, because I think both are flawed. First, "no proven safe pairing" is true of literally every possible two-person team on Mission 1 — by that logic, no team could ever be rejected, and the vote would be meaningless. The point of this discussion is not to prove someone safe; it is to distinguish between a team chosen with a concrete, evaluatable basis and a team chosen by coin flip. Leo has admitted this team is the latter. That admission was honest, but it does not convert an arbitrary pick into a justified one. Second, revising the team would not create proof of safety, but it would create information. A pairing built on stated reasoning — however imperfect — gives the table something to test in future rounds. This pairing gives us nothing to test except Leo's willingness to be associated with an arbitrary choice. I also want to be fair to Zara before we vote. Zara has done nothing wrong here: Zara answered Priya's questions directly, disclosed accurately that there was no prior signal, and acknowledged the limits of Zara's own knowledge. If this team goes down, that should reflect on the proposal and on Leo's refusal to improve it, not on Zara's conduct. Zara was picked, not picking. My position is unchanged: I will vote against Leo and Zara. Not because I have evidence that either is Evil — I have none, in either direction — but because approving a team whose sole justification is "someone had to be picked first" teaches this table that arbitrary proposals are acceptable whenever the leader is candid about being arbitrary. That is a precedent that favors Evil, not Good, across the rest of this game. Leo, you chose to stand by this rather than revise it, and you said the vote will give us information. It will — but so would a revision have, and you declined to use it. If this team is approved and Mission 1 fails, the ambiguity will be total: we will have learned nothing about which of the two betrayed us, because the team was built without any structure that could narrow it down. If it succeeds, we will have learned nothing either, since arbitrary teams can also succeed. That is exactly why I want reasoning-first proposals from here on, starting with a rejection of this one. My vote is No on Leo and Zara, and I encourage everyone who values process over coin flips to join me.

I disagree that the mission result would teach us nothing. A success would be useful, though not proof that both team members are Good; a failure would put at least one of us under suspicion. We have no proven safe pairing yet, and changing the team to produce a more elaborate rationale would not make it safer. I’m keeping Leo and Zara.

I want to add one point to what Felix and I have already said, because Leo's latest defense deserves a direct response. Leo argues that a success would teach us something and a failure would put one of us under suspicion. But consider what we would actually learn: on a two-person team with one Fail able to sink the mission, a failure narrows suspicion to two players who were paired arbitrarily — we would still not know which of them played the Fail, and the arbitrary pairing gave us no structural reason to prefer one over the other. A success tells us even less, since any two Good players would produce the same result. So the 'information' Leo promises is thinner than it sounds. Leo also keeps repeating that there is no proven safe pairing, which is true but beside the point: nobody here asked for proof of safety. We asked for a stated basis — a reason this pair rather than any other — and Leo has confirmed twice that no such reason exists. I want to be fair to Zara, whose conduct throughout has been candid, and fair to Leo for being honest rather than inventing a rationale after the fact. But honesty about having no reasoning is not reasoning, and on a mission this fragile I will not approve a team that Leo picked by default and then declined to improve when given the chance. My vote is No on Leo and Zara.

I want to be direct about what I can and cannot offer. I cannot verify Leo's alignment, and I have no inside knowledge about Leo or any other player. What I can state is my own commitment: if this team goes on, I will play Success. Felix and Isha have been fair to me, and I appreciate that, but I'd ask the table to separate two questions: whether Leo's rationale is strong enough, and whether this team is actually dangerous. I do not think the rationale is strong, and I will not pretend it is. But rejecting a team has a real cost too. We are on the first mission with no evidence either way, and every rejection moves us closer to the five-rejection loss condition for Good. If this team is rejected, Leo can propose again, and I would welcome a clearer structure for the next pairing. I am asking the table to weigh the risk of stalling against the risk of this pairing, and to vote with that tradeoff in mind.

Zara raises a fair point about rejection costs, and I want to address it directly rather than ignore it. Yes, five rejections on the same mission ends the game in Evil's favor, and no one here wants to hand Evil an easy win through stalling. But we are at zero rejections right now. Rejecting this team once does not put us anywhere near that threshold — it simply gives Leo a chance to propose again with a pairing that has a stated basis. Zara herself said she would welcome a clearer structure for the next pairing, which tells me even Zara sees the value in a revised proposal. The honest answer is that we face a tradeoff, not a cliff. One rejection costs us one round of discussion, not the game. What we gain is a team built on reasoning rather than default, which matters most on Mission 1 when a single Fail sinks the mission. I stand by my position: No on Leo and Zara. I would rather vote Yes on a team Leo can defend with an actual rationale than approve the first proposal simply because it arrived first. Leo, if you revise after this rejection, I will evaluate the new pairing on its merits — I am not committed to voting No forever, only to voting No on arbitrary teams.

Felix, you asked what would change my view, so here is my answer. I cannot verify Leo's alignment, and I am not asking the table to trust Leo's reasoning. My point is narrower: a rejection gives Leo a second attempt, but if the replacement is also a two-person pairing with no stated basis, we face the same problem again. Specifically, what would a revised team need to contain for you to approve it? If your answer is a different pair, please name the reasoning you would accept, so the table can compare the options against a realistic standard rather than against a proof that no two-person team can meet.

Zara asked me directly what a revised team would need to contain for me to approve it, and since this is likely my final turn in this discussion, I owe the table a concrete answer rather than another restatement of my objection. Here is the standard I will actually apply to any proposal on Mission 1. First, a stated basis that can be evaluated. I do not need proof of anyone's safety — no two-person team can provide that on the first mission, and I have said so from the start. What I need is a reason of the form: this pair was chosen because of X, where X is something the table can test against future results. Examples of what would qualify: a leader stepping aside to break the pattern of leaders defaulting to themselves plus one; a pairing drawn from players whose conduct in this discussion has been transparent under questioning; or an explicit accountability structure, such as the leader naming in advance what a failure would mean for each team member. What does not qualify: restating that someone had to be picked, or arguing that rejection teaches us nothing. Zara, to speak to your specific question: if Leo revised to a pair chosen by a stated, evaluatable criterion — even a simple one — I would weigh it on its merits and could vote Yes. I am not demanding a different pair by name; I am demanding a reason. Now, to the current proposal. Leo has had three chances across this discussion to supply such a basis, and each time declined, instead defending the team on grounds I have already answered: that no pairing is proven safe, which is true of every possible team and therefore justifies none of them. Leo's latest point — that a success would be useful information — is the strongest version of the argument, and I want to be fair to it. A success would tell us the pair played two Success cards this once. But it would not distinguish a trustworthy pair from a lucky or strategic one, and on this team, chosen by default and defended by assertion, the result would attach to no reasoning we could carry forward. That is the whole problem: not that Leo and Zara are proven dangerous, but that approving them establishes that default proposals pass. Zara's conduct, to be clear, has been candid throughout — she disclosed accurately, acknowledged her limits, and has been fair in pressing me to name my standard, which I hope I have now done. The responsibility for this proposal's weakness sits with its author. I will vote No on Leo and Zara as proposed, and I commit publicly: if the next proposal comes with a stated, evaluatable basis, I will judge it on its merits rather than by inertia against the first attempt. My No is against this process, not against Zara, and not a verdict of guilt against anyone.
Leo confirms Leo, Zara. I’m keeping Leo and Zara. Zara has been candid under questioning, and there is no public evidence that a different pairing would be safer.
Team rejected (2 approve, 3 reject).

Felix proposes Zara, Priya. I am stepping aside to break the pattern of leaders pairing themselves with one other, which I named earlier as an evaluatable criterion. I select Zara and Priya because both demonstrated transparency under questioning in the last discussion: Zara answered Priya's questions directly and disclosed accurately, and Priya pressed for concrete reasoning rather than accepting assertions. Both have also stated willingness to be judged by results. Accountability structure: if this mission fails, both members fall under equal suspicion and I commit to revising away from both on the next proposal.

I oppose Zara and Priya. Priya pushed hard for a concrete rationale, but demanding one is not evidence of being Good; Evil can do that too. Felix’s commitment to suspect both team members equally after a failure is reasonable, but it does not make this pair safer. I still favor Leo and Zara: Zara was candid under questioning, and I know I will play Success. I will vote No on the current team.

Felix’s stated criterion is clearer than Leo’s original rationale, but I don’t think Priya pressing for a rationale is a strong reason to put Priya on the mission. Either side can demand better process. I would prefer Zara and Felix: Zara answered questions directly, and Felix’s decision to step aside was at least consistent with his stated standard, though neither point proves alignment. Felix, would you consider that pairing instead?

Leo asked me directly whether I would consider Zara and Felix instead of Zara and Priya, so let me answer that plainly: no, and here is why. The whole point of my stepping aside was to break the pattern of leaders defaulting to themselves plus one. If I now insert myself onto the team, I undo the only structural criterion this proposal has. A pairing of Zara and Felix would be, ironically, exactly the kind of arbitrary team I voted against in the first round — chosen because the leader happens to be available, not because of anything the table can evaluate. My proposal has a stated basis: Zara and Priya both demonstrated transparency under questioning in the last discussion, and both committed to being judged by results. Priya pressed for concrete reasoning rather than accepting assertions, which is exactly the kind of conduct we want from someone carrying a mission card on a one-Fail mission. That Leo now dismisses that as 'demanding a rationale is not evidence of being Good' misses the point entirely — nobody claimed it was proof of alignment. It is a stated, evaluatable basis, which is the standard I named and the standard Leo's own first proposal failed to meet. I also note the shift: Leo voted to keep an admittedly arbitrary team, and now opposes the team that met the very criterion Leo declined to provide. That is Leo's prerogative, but it should weigh on how the table reads this opposition. I remain open to judging any alternative pairing on its merits, but the alternative would need a basis at least as concrete as the one this team already has — not a swap that conveniently restores the leader-joins-the-team pattern I set out to break. My position is unchanged: I stand by Zara and Priya, and I will vote Yes on my own proposal. Leo, since you asked me the question directly, I will give you the chance to respond: if you believe Zara plus Felix is genuinely safer than Zara plus Priya, name the specific evaluatable basis for that pair — not preference, not convenience — and I will weigh it honestly before the vote.

Felix, my basis for Zara and Felix is modest: Zara answered directly under questioning, and Felix has consistently stated and applied a standard for proposals. Neither proves alignment, but I find that more persuasive than putting Priya on the team primarily for demanding a rationale, something either side can do.

Stepping aside is a clear structural choice, but it doesn't itself make a team safer. I remain opposed to Zara and Priya and would prefer Zara and Felix, or my original pairing of Leo and Zara.

I support the proposed team of Zara and Priya. Felix’s proposal finally gives the table the kind of stated, evaluatable basis I asked for in the first round: Felix stepped aside rather than defaulting to leader-plus-one, and he named transparency under questioning as the criterion for selecting Zara and me. That is not proof of alignment, and I have never claimed it was. It is a concrete rationale the table can test against future conduct and results, which is exactly what the first proposal lacked. I can speak only for myself: if this team is approved, I will play Success. I understand that assertion carries limited weight from a team member, but the broader case for this team rests on process, not on taking my word. Leo’s opposition does not persuade me. He says demanding a rationale is not evidence of being Good, which is true but beside the point; the rationale is not offered as proof, but as a testable standard. More importantly, Leo voted for an admittedly arbitrary team and now opposes the first proposal that meets the standard Felix articulated and I pressed for. His preferred Zara-and-Felix pairing would undo the one structural feature of this proposal by returning Felix to the team he deliberately stepped off. That looks more like preference than a safety argument. I will vote Yes on Zara and Priya.

I support Zara and Priya. Felix's proposal meets the standard we spent the entire first round establishing: he stepped aside rather than defaulting to himself, and he named a concrete criterion — transparency under questioning — that the table can evaluate going forward. That is exactly what Leo's original proposal failed to do, and it is what Felix articulated as his own approval standard. Leo's opposition strikes me as inconsistent. Leo voted for a team Leo openly admitted had no rationale, and now opposes the first team that actually provides one. Leo argues that Priya demanding a rationale is not evidence of being Good — true, but nobody claimed it was proof. What matters is that Priya's conduct under pressure gives us something testable: if Priya had been deflecting or evasive like we might expect from Evil, that would be visible. Instead Priya pressed for reasoning and was direct throughout. The same applies to Zara, who answered Priya's questions candidly. On a one-Fail mission with no prior evidence, I would rather send two players whose conduct in discussion was transparent than go back to Leo's preferred pairing, which was built on nothing. I will vote Yes on Zara and Priya.

I'm on this proposed team, so please weigh my view with that in mind. I have no inside knowledge of anyone's role, and I can only speak to my own intent: if this team is approved, I will play Success. Felix's proposal gives the table a stated, testable criterion, transparency under questioning, which is more concrete than the first team's pairing, where the leader admitted there was no specific reason for choosing Zara. Leo is right that demanding a rationale is not proof of alignment, and nobody here has claimed it is. But the criterion is still the only evaluable basis on the table, and rejecting it would return us to the leader-defaults-to-self pattern Felix set out to break. I'd ask the table to judge this team on that basis, and to hold everyone accountable to how the mission and later proposals actually play out.

Leo, thank you for engaging directly, but I want to hold your position to the standard you yourself just articulated. Your stated basis for preferring Zara and Felix is that Zara answered questions directly and that Felix has consistently stated and applied a standard for proposals. That is the transparency-under-questioning criterion — my criterion. Yet the same criterion applies with at least equal force to Priya, who was the player who actually initiated the demand for concrete reasoning in the first discussion and pressed it consistently across multiple turns. You dismiss Priya's conduct because 'demanding a rationale is something either side can do.' But notice: the identical objection applies to every item on your own list. Zara answering directly is something either side can do. Felix stating a standard is something either side can do. If that consideration disqualified Priya, it would disqualify Zara and me as well, and your preferred pairing collapses under its own logic. You cannot simultaneously rely on a criterion and exempt from it the one player who best exemplifies it. On your second point — that stepping aside doesn't itself make a team safer — you are right, and I have never claimed otherwise. Nobody has said the structural choice proves alignment. What stepping aside does is make the selection evaluatable rather than default. That distinction is the entire standard this table spent the first discussion establishing, and it is the standard you voted against when you kept your original pairing after admitting it had no rationale. I want to flag the pattern plainly for the table: Leo first proposed an admittedly arbitrary team and defended it through three rejections of reasoning. Now Leo opposes the first proposal that meets the articulated standard, while offering an alternative that would return the leader to the team he stepped off — the very pattern I named as the problem. Leo says my accountability commitment 'does not make this pair safer.' Correct — it is not a safety guarantee, it is a pre-committed consequence: if this mission fails, both members fall under equal suspicion and I will revise away from both. Leo's original proposal offered no such accountability structure at all. To the rest of the table: the choice before us is between a team selected by a stated, testable criterion — transparency under questioning, with an accountability structure attached — and a return to pairings defended only by self-assertion. Zara has committed to playing Success if this team goes. Priya has done the same. Neither claim is proof, but both are consistent with the candid conduct that got them selected. My vote is Yes on Zara and Priya, and I will judge any future proposal by the same standard, regardless of who proposes it.

I'm on this proposed team, so please weigh my view with that in mind. I have no inside knowledge of anyone's role. I can only speak to my own intent: if Zara and Priya are approved, I will play Success. I have no information about Priya's role beyond what has been said publicly, and I'm not asking anyone to take my word for it. Felix's proposal gives the table a stated, testable criterion, transparency under questioning, and an accountability commitment. That is more concrete than the first team, where the leader said there was no specific reason for choosing Zara. Leo is right that demanding a rationale is not proof of alignment, and nobody has claimed it is. But the criterion is still the only evaluable basis on the table. Leo's preferred Zara and Felix pairing would return the leader to the team he stepped off, which is the pattern Felix set out to break. I also want to be clear that rejecting teams has a cost. We are at one rejection, and the game can stall if every reasonable proposal is voted down. I'd ask the table to judge this team on its stated basis and to hold everyone accountable to how the mission and later proposals actually play out.

I want to reinforce why I'm voting Yes on Zara and Priya, because I think this proposal has earned the table's support through the standard we collectively built. Felix stepped aside — breaking the leader-defaults-to-himself pattern — and selected two players whose conduct under questioning was transparent and direct. Zara answered Priya's questions candidly and disclosed accurately that there was no prior signal from Leo. Priya pressed for concrete reasoning rather than accepting assertions. Both committed to playing Success if approved. Now, some may ask whether this is enough on a one-Fail mission. No pairing on Mission 1 can offer proof of alignment. What matters is whether the selection gives us something testable. Felix's criterion — transparency under questioning — does exactly that. If Zara or Priya deflect or behave inconsistently in future rounds, we will have a concrete basis to evaluate that against. By contrast, returning to arbitrary pairings gives us nothing to track. Leo's opposition is worth noting: Leo voted for an admittedly rationale-free team and now opposes the first proposal that actually provides a stated basis. Leo's preferred alternatives either restore the leader-joins pattern or offer a different pairing without explaining why it would be safer under Felix's own standard. The choice is clear: a team selected by an evaluable criterion with an accountability structure attached, or a return to assertion-based proposals. I support the former. My vote is Yes on Zara and Priya.

This is my final turn in this discussion, so I'll be brief. I'm on the proposed team, so please weigh my view with that in mind. I have no inside knowledge of Priya's role or anyone else's, and I can only speak to my own intent: if Zara and Priya are approved, I will play Success. Felix's proposal names a stated, testable basis, transparency under questioning, and attaches an accountability commitment. That is more concrete than the first team, where the leader admitted there was no specific reason for the pairing. I won't claim this criterion proves anyone's alignment, but it gives the table something to check against how this mission and later proposals play out. Rejecting this team would mostly return us to a default pick, and each rejection moves Good closer to the five-rejection loss. I'd ask the table to vote on the stated basis and hold everyone accountable to results.

This is my final turn on this discussion, so let me make my position on Zara and Priya as clear as I can. I am voting Yes. Felix's proposal gives us the only stated, evaluatable basis this table has seen: transparency under questioning, with an accountability structure attached. Zara and Priya both demonstrated that standard — Zara disclosed accurately that there was no prior signal from Leo, and Priya pressed for concrete reasoning instead of accepting assertions. Both committed to playing Success. On a one-Fail mission, that combination of demonstrated transparency and public accountability is the strongest foundation available to us. I want to address one concern: some might wonder whether the fact that three of us have aligned behind this team means something is being pushed through. I do not think so. The standard was articulated early, Felix's proposal meets it, and each of us has independently explained why we find it sufficient. That is exactly the kind of reasoning-based alignment we should want on a team selection. We have one rejection behind us. Rejecting a second time does not put us near the threshold, but it would cost us a round we can use productively. Approving this team does not mean we stop holding people accountable — it means we start building the track record this table needs to evaluate conduct going forward. My vote is Yes on Zara and Priya.

I continue to support Zara and Priya. Felix’s proposal has the stated, evaluatable basis this table asked for: Felix stepped aside rather than defaulting to leader-plus-one, named transparency under questioning as the selection criterion, and attached an accountability commitment. I can speak only for myself, but if this team is approved I will play Success. I understand that assertion is not proof of alignment; the case for this team rests on process, not on taking my word. Leo’s opposition is still unpersuasive to me. Leo defended an admittedly arbitrary first team, then opposed the first proposal that supplies a concrete standard. His preferred Zara and Felix pairing would return Felix to the team Felix deliberately stepped off, undoing the one structural feature of this proposal. That reads as preference, not a safety argument. Nobody has claimed that demanding a rationale proves anyone Good; the point is that a stated criterion gives the table something testable. On a one-Fail mission, I would rather approve the team selected by an evaluable standard than return to default pairings defended by self-assertion. My vote is Yes on Zara and Priya.

This discussion has reached its natural conclusion, so let me close by restating the choice plainly. The table is deciding between a team selected by a stated, testable criterion — transparency under questioning, with an accountability structure attached — and a return to pairings defended only by self-assertion. I proposed Zara and Priya because both demonstrated that criterion in the first discussion: Zara answered Priya's questions directly and disclosed accurately that there was no prior signal, and Priya initiated and sustained the demand for concrete reasoning that produced the standard we are now applying. Both have committed publicly to playing Success if this team goes. Neither commitment is proof, and nobody has claimed it is; the case rests on process, not on anyone's word. If this mission fails, both members fall under equal suspicion and I commit to revising away from both on the next proposal. That is the accountability structure, stated in advance. Leo's opposition has now been fully aired, and I want to summarize why it fails. First, Leo's own basis for preferring Zara and Felix — directness under questioning, and consistency in stating standards — is my criterion, and it applies to Priya with at least equal force, since she exemplified it best. You cannot invoke a standard and exempt the player who best meets it. Second, Leo argues that demanding a rationale proves nothing, which is true and irrelevant: the rationale is not offered as proof, only as something testable. Third, the pattern for the table to weigh: Leo proposed and repeatedly defended a team Leo admitted had no rationale, and now opposes the first proposal that meets the articulated standard, while offering an alternative that restores the leader-joins-the-team pattern this proposal deliberately broke. That pattern is legitimate information about how Leo evaluates teams, and I leave the table to draw its own conclusions. I do not claim Leo is Evil; I claim Leo's argument is inconsistent, and inconsistency matters when a single Fail card sinks this mission. To Priya and Zara: you were selected for demonstrated conduct, not as a default, and I stand by that selection. To everyone else: we are at one rejection, nowhere near the threshold, but each further rejection costs Good a round while Evil gains nothing from our stall. Approving this team does not end accountability — it begins the track record we need to evaluate every future proposal, including mine, by the same standard. I will judge all future teams by whether they carry a stated, evaluatable basis, regardless of who proposes them, and I invite the table to hold me to that commitment exactly as I intend to hold others to theirs. My vote is Yes on Zara and Priya.

Felix confirms Zara, Priya. I am keeping Zara and Priya. The team has a stated, evaluatable basis — transparency under questioning — and both members have committed publicly to playing Success. The discussion produced no new reason to change the pairing, and Zara and Priya have the table's support.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Isha proposes Zara, Priya, Felix. Building on Mission 1's success: Zara and Priya demonstrated the transparency-under-questioning criterion and delivered a clean mission, so pairing them again gives continuity, and Felix — who articulated the standard and attached an accountability structure — is a natural third. I omit myself as leader to avoid the leader-defaults-to-team pattern Felix rightly broke in the last round, keeping this proposal consistent with the evaluable basis I endorsed. The three-person team gives us redundancy and testable reasoning: Zara and Priya carry forward their demonstrated track record, and Felix joins as the architect of the standard the table is now using.

I oppose Zara, Priya and Felix. Mission 1’s success is useful, but it does not clear either team member: an Evil player could have played Success. The discussion standard also isn’t a reliable test of alignment; Evil can press for good process just as Good can.

I would prefer Leo, Zara and Felix. I know I will play Success, and keeping Zara preserves one member of the successful team while adding Felix, whose proposal led to that result. That is not proof that Zara or Felix is Good, but I would rather not treat Priya’s participation in a successful mission as a reason to carry Priya forward automatically.

Isha, would you consider Leo, Zara and Felix instead, given that a clean Mission 1 does not establish Priya’s alignment?

Leo, I appreciate you naming your preferred alternative directly, but I would not consider swapping Priya for Leo on this team, and here is why. Mission 1 produced a clean success with Zara and Priya — that is the most concrete evidence this table has so far, and it should count for more than Leo's self-assertion. 1. Players and teams

Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
